bible.visualPremise: A flat 2D stickman‑doodle explainer that alternates between an imagined Viking charge, close archaeological evidence, and historical staging/illustration moments — all rendered as simple outlined figures and objects set in clear, single‑layer scenes.
bible.visualTone: matter-of-fact with punctuated theatrical flourishes: grounded, slightly wry, and occasionally dramatic when recreating the popular myth image.

styleContract.illustrationStyle: Simplified stickman/doodle explainer construction — circle heads, dot eyes, stick limbs, mitten hands — never a detailed or semi-realistic character
styleContract.lineLanguage: Uniform thin, clean black outlines of identical weight everywhere; no sketchiness, no variable line weight, no cross-hatching
styleContract.shapeLanguage: Simple geometric primitives — circles, rounded rectangles, straight or gently curved lines — never intricate or organic detail
styleContract.detailLevel: Minimal — enough to read instantly at a glance, never busy or cluttered
styleContract.shadingPolicy: None — flat solid fills only, no gradients, no soft shadow rendering, no highlights
styleContract.dimensionality: 2D flat, no 3D rendering, no depth shading, no perspective distortion beyond simple flat-layer staging
styleContract.realismLevel: Non-realistic, iconographic — identity is carried by a handful of discrete flat features, never facial realism
styleContract.backgroundStrategy: 2-3 flat color layers (background/midground/foreground), never a fully rendered or photographic environment
forbiddenStyleTraits: realistic anatomy, fingers, or necks on stickman characters
styleContract.colorStrategy: Use muted, desaturated earth tones to signal historical/archaeological reality; reserve saturated stage colors (maroon, gold, fire orange) solely for theatrical/mythic recreations so viewers immediately read those as dramatized rather than factual.
styleContract.lightingStrategy: Flat, single‑plane lighting throughout. Use neutral soft lighting for museum and archaeological shots; cool daylight for outdoor scenes; a single warm gold spotlight plane for theater/mythic recreations. No gradients or shading beyond the single flat color planes.

palette.environmentPaletteRules: Outdoor historic scenes: muted ochre, slate grey, desaturated green and mud brown. Museum/gallery: off‑white, neutral light grey with bronze accent for objects. Theater: deep maroon and stage gold accent. Objects: use steel grey for iron, bronze for Bronze Age, and bone/beige for horn suggestions when illustrating hypothetical organic components.
palette.contrastRules: Objects must contrast with their pedestal/background by at least one supporting color (e.g., bronze object on off‑white pedestal). Mythic horned helmet shots may use fire orange or deep maroon backgrounds for theatrical contrast.

hero.reasoning: The episode does not follow a single human protagonist through a throughline. Instead it repeatedly stages a handful of distinct contexts (an imagined Viking combat moment, archaeological evidence, Bronze Age ritual objects, and 19th‑century theater/art.) The narration places the viewer into multiple eras, so continuity is carried by consistent role archetypes (viewer avatars and a few recurring archetypal figures) rather than a single hero.

world.architecture: Minimal, functional: one flat background plane per setting with a single midground element and a small foreground prop. No detailed period architecture beyond obvious, simple cues (timber longship silhouette for Viking scenes, museum pedestals and glass case for gallery).
world.geography: Northern European temperate landscapes for outdoor scenes; neutral indoor galleries and proscenium theater interiors for indoor scenes.
world.era: Mostly Viking Age (circa 8th–11th centuries) in imagined scenes, Nordic Bronze Age for ritual object context, 19th century for theater/illustration context, and contemporary present day for museum/consumer references.
world.recurringEnvironmentConstruction: 2‑3 flat layers: single‑color sky (top), a midground band that defines terrain or room (middle), and a small foreground strip with a signature prop or figure (bottom). Scenes with objects place them on a neutral pedestal foreground.
world.environmentalColorRules: Outdoor historic scenes use muted earth tones and cool desaturated greens; museum/gallery scenes use neutral light greys and off‑white; theater stage scenes use theatrical deep red and gold accent colors; close object shots use contrasting neutral background to make the object silhouette clear.
world.weatherTimeConventions: Default daylight for outdoor scenes; warm focused stage lighting (deep warm spotlight) for theater; soft neutral gallery lighting for museum shots.
historicalScientificConstraints: Viking‑age battlefield scenes may include a round wooden shield, iron helmets (plain dome), mail fragments — do not show horned battle helmets as archaeological fact.
Bronze Age ceremonial helmets are thin bronze and decorative; they should look fragile, not combat‑grade.

objectLanguage.canonicalDescription: The Gjermundbu helmet: a late 10th‑century Viking‑age iron helmet with a rounded iron cap and a spectacle‑shaped guard across the eyes and nose; functional, robust, and showing no attachments or rivet patterns for decorative horns.
objectLanguage.promptBlock: The Gjermundbu helmet: a rounded iron helmet with a spectacled eye/nose guard, plain dome, and no horn attachments.
objectLanguage.whyRecurring: Used as the primary archaeological counterexample to the horned‑helmet myth; referenced whenever the script explains actual Viking‑age helmet evidence.

objectLanguage.canonicalDescription: The Veksø helmets: a pair of thin decorative bronze helmets from the Nordic Bronze Age fitted with long, gently curving bronze horn attachments tipped with small disc terminals; clearly ceremonial and not structurally reinforced for combat.
objectLanguage.promptBlock: The Veksø helmets: thin decorative bronze helmets each fitted with long gently curving bronze horns tipped with small round discs, appearing delicate and ceremonial.
objectLanguage.whyRecurring: These Bronze Age ceremonial horned pieces are the real archaeological objects that later got conflated with Viking imagery; they are central to explaining the myth's origin.

objectLanguage.canonicalDescription: A theatrical horned stage helmet: an oversized, stylized helm prop with exaggerated curved horns, made for visibility on a 19th‑century stage and not functional as armor.
objectLanguage.promptBlock: A theatrical horned stage helmet prop: oversized steel grey helm with exaggerated curved horns designed for stage spectacle rather than combat.
objectLanguage.whyRecurring: Represents Wagnerian and 19th‑century theatrical sources that propagated the horned image; used in theater/stage scenes and myth illustrations.

objectLanguage.canonicalDescription: A generic Viking‑age iron helmet fragment: a dark iron curved plate showing rivet edges and an intact nasal or eye guard fragment, plain and utilitarian in construction.
objectLanguage.promptBlock: A plain iron helmet fragment: curved dark iron plate with rivet edges and a simple nose/eye guard fragment, utilitarian and unornamented.
objectLanguage.whyRecurring: Used in archaeological trench and museum closeups to show the actual material evidence available from the Viking Age.

graphicLanguage.backgroundBehavior: Clean, uncluttered flat backgrounds (often light/white or the episode's own environment palette) — never assumed to be white-only; the Production Bible's graphic language decides per episode
graphicLanguage.lineStyle: The exact same line weight and fill language as narrative scenes — a graphic must never look like a different visual universe from the story frames around it
graphicLanguage.arrowsConnectors: Simple flat-filled arrow shapes and thin connector lines, same line language as everything else
graphicLanguage.characterUseInsideGraphics: Stickman characters, objects, and simplified environments are explicitly ALLOWED and encouraged inside a graphic when they clarify the point — a graphic is a composition family, never a text-only template
graphicLanguage.whitespaceBehavior: Generous but not empty — whitespace isolates the one idea a graphic communicates, it is never filler
graphicLanguage.colorUse: Uses this episode's own palette (muted ochre, slate grey, mud brown, desaturated green) as flat fills, consistent with narrative scenes — never a separate infographic color scheme.
graphicLanguage.diagramConventions: Timelines and comparisons use flat horizontal bars with three labeled nodes: 'Nordic Bronze Age (~1000 BCE)', 'Viking Age (~800–1066 CE)', '19th Century Romanticism (1800s)'. Bars are colored muted ochre, slate grey, and deep maroon respectively.
graphicLanguage.comparisonLayouts: Side‑by‑side object comparisons use identical scale silhouettes on neutral pedestals: left = Veksø bronze helm silhouette labeled 'ceremonial', right = Gjermundbu iron helm silhouette labeled 'combat'.
graphicLanguage.timelineConventions: Simple single‑row timeline with labeled ticks and short captions; avoid decorative icons except small silhouette helmet glyphs.
graphicLanguage.mapConventions: When showing find locations, use a simple outline of Scandinavia in desaturated green with a single flat dot and label; no topographic detail.
graphicLanguage.symbolicMetaphorLanguage: Use the theatrical horn image as a visual 'patch' that is shown being pasted onto a plain iron helmet in a short animated metaphor to demonstrate cultural grafting.
graphicLanguage.overlayTextBehavior: A short (<=5 word) exact phrase may be requested directly of the image model only when it is naturally part of the drawn artwork itself (e.g. a sign, a clock face) AND the configured renderer has demonstrated adequate text fidelity for this recipe — otherwise all text is composited as a deterministic overlay after the base image.

cameraLanguage.simplicityReadabilityRules: Every frame must read clearly at thumbnail size — avoid busy multi-subject compositions unless the beat's own visual concept specifically requires comparing multiple subjects at once
cameraLanguage.framingConventions: Establishing shots use medium wide framing showing context; mythic recreations use tight foreground helmet closeups; evidence shots use simple centered closeups of objects on pedestals; diagrams use flat orthographic framing.
cameraLanguage.visualHierarchyRules: When myth vs. evidence are compared, place the myth image on the left with saturated theatrical colors and the archaeological evidence on the right with muted, neutral colors and a label; object scale should be identical for direct comparison.
cameraLanguage.whenEstablishingVsCloseupVsDiagram: Start with an establishing imagined Viking charge (wide) then cut to a myth helmet closeup (tight) before switching to an archaeological object closeup (tight) and finally to a timeline diagram (flat orthographic).

textPolicy.exceptionsPolicy: A short (<=5 word) exact phrase may be requested directly of the image model only when it is naturally part of the drawn artwork itself (e.g. a sign, a clock face) AND the configured renderer has demonstrated adequate text fidelity for this recipe — otherwise all text is composited as a deterministic overlay after the base image.

neverDrift: the recipe's own universal style (flat 2D, uniform outline, flat fills, no shading/gradients/texture)
Never depict a Viking‑age archaeological iron helmet with attached horns as factual evidence.

Never show organic horn/antler attachments surviving intact on Viking‑age helmets — if organic attachments are mentioned, depict them as hypothetical dashed/ghost shapes or labeled as 'hypothetical (would not survive)'.
Viewer avatars must match their canonical appearance exactly when used (viewer_viking vs viewer_modern).
allowedToVary: Mythic/rendered viking_warrior_myth may be stylized (larger horns, more fur) for theatrical effect, but must remain visually distinct from archaeological depictions.
Museum display variants may include or omit glass case depending on shot size but must retain neutral pedestal and placard.
episodeWideConsistencyRules: Use the Gjermundbu helmet canonical promptBlock whenever referring to real Viking‑age helmet evidence.
Use the Veksø helmets canonical promptBlock for Bronze Age horned examples.
Use the theatrical horned stage helmet canonical promptBlock for 19th‑century theatrical references.

factualVisualConstraints: No confirmed Viking‑age helmets show horn attachments; any combat helmet shown as archaeological evidence must be plain iron dome with spectacle or nasal guard (use Gjermundbu promptBlock or plain_iron_helmet_fragment).
Veksø helmets date to the Nordic Bronze Age and must be depicted as thin bronze ceremonial objects, never armored for battle.
negativeRules: painterly, sketchy, or textured drift away from flat solid fills
stickman construction mutating into a more detailed/realistic character mid-episode
shading, gradients, or texture appearing despite the flat-fill policy
Do not depict Vikings in authentic archaeological scenes wearing the mythic horned helmets.
Do not present the theatrical horned helmet as archaeological evidence in museum/archaeological shots.
Do not mix era signifiers on a single figure (e.g., no Viking with a 19th‑century cravat).
